pages.body_text: The Anatomy of a Hyperlink Citation Ranking Engine Prof. Harold Vance and David Chen Department of Computer Science, Redwood State University Technical Report RSU-CS-98-09 -- September 4, 1998 Abstract. Existing commercial search engines rely primarily on term frequency, keyword proximity, and author-supplied META tags, leaving them vulnerable to keyword spamming across the rapidly growing 1998 World Wide Web. We present the Redwood BackRub/PageRank prototype, which computes an objective global authority vector over the hyperlink graph via a damped random surfer model (damping factor d = 0.85) combined with an inverted full-text and anchor-text index. 1. Introduction & The Keyword Spam Problem As the Web expands past 150 million HTML documents, naive lexical matching returns hundreds of low-value results on broad queries such as "linux" or "recipes." pages.body_text: CS 404 Lecture Notes: Eigenvectors of the World Wide Web Graph Prof. Harold Vance | Lecture 7 -- Updated 09-Sep-1998 Today we analyze why power iteration converges rapidly on the Web adjacency matrix. Let M be the column-stochastic hyperlink matrix where M[i,j] = 1/outdeg(j) if page j links to page i. pages.body_text: Distributed Web Crawling in C++ and Solaris Threads Prof. Harold Vance | Systems Note -- 02-Sep-1998 Fetching millions of pages over university T3 lines requires asynchronous non-blocking sockets paired with a Solaris libthread worker pool. Each worker holds up to 64 concurrent HTTP/1.0 GET descriptors, caches DNS lookups locally to avoid saturating our BIND 8 resolver, and enforces a 15-second per-host politeness gap alongside strict /robots.txt exclusion rules. struct CrawlFrontierEntry { uint64_t url_md5_hi; /* 64-bit MD5 deduplication key */ uint32_t host_hash; /* per-server politeness bucket */ char url[512]; }; Our URL frontier strips session IDs and infinite CGI calendar loops to avoid crawler traps. pages.body_text: Y2K vs Year 2038: struct tm Pitfalls in Legacy C Code Prof. Elena Rostova | Redwood Y2K Engineering Note While POSIX 32-bit time_t stores seconds since January 1, 1970 and does not wrap to negative values until January 19, 2038 (03:14:07 UTC), thousands of C programs still break on January 1, 2000 because developers formatted tm->tm_year with "19%02d" instead of "%04d", tm->tm_year + 1900. /* WRONG: prints '19100' on Jan 1, 2000! */ printf("Year: 19%02d\n", tm_now->tm_year); /* RIGHT: tm_year is years since 1900 (100 in 2000) */ printf("Year: %04d\n", tm_now->tm_year + 1900); Soda Hall Support & Quick Checklist: Before emailing helpdesk@cs.redwood.edu, verify disk blocks with quota -v, confirm your NFS automount path under /home/grad or /usr/local/bin, and record the SPARCstation hostname printed on the bezel. pages.body_text: Borealis Linux Year 2000 Readiness & BIOS RTC Statement Borealis Linux 5.2 Documentation Project | Updated 11-Sep-1998 Y2K Readiness: Linux kernel time_t counts signed 32-bit seconds since Jan 1, 1970, meaning Year 2000 poses zero kernel rollover risk (POSIX epoch wraps Jan 19, 2038). However, older Award/AMI PC BIOS real-time clocks (RTC) can boot to 1900 or 1980 after Dec 31, 1999. pages.body_text: [borealis-dev] Re: SMP spinlock deadlock - test patch attached (works on Tyan Tiger) From: kernel-hacker@northstar.net (Martin Lind) To: borealis-dev@lists.penguinos.org Date: Fri, 04 Sep 1998 13:31:07 -0700 Subject: [borealis-dev] Re: SMP spinlock deadlock - test patch attached (works on Tyan Tiger) Message-ID: <199809041331.B0083@lists.penguinos.org> X-List: Borealis Linux 5.2 Technical Discussion (doc_0083) X-Mailing-List: <borealis-dev@lists.penguinos.org> archive/majordomo 1.94.4 > Try booting with `noapic` first, or enable the APIC NMI watchdog timer... Found it! The NMI watchdog caught a lock inversion between `dcache_lock` and `wait_on_inode` in fs/dcache.c on 2.1.120. Attached one-line patch moves spin_unlock above the schedule() call. Survived 6 hours of `make -j8` on Tyan Tiger 100! --- linux/fs/dcache.c.orig Wed Sep 2 11:04:12 1998 +++...

pages.body_text: [borealis-dev] Re: Y2K RTC rollover - Linux time_t safe until 2038 From: pnovak@penguinos.org (Petr Novak) To: borealis-dev@lists.penguinos.org Date: Fri, 04 Sep 1998 12:29:53 -0700 Subject: [borealis-dev] Re: Y2K RTC rollover - Linux time_t safe until 2038 Message-ID: <199809041229.B0097@lists.penguinos.org> X-List: Borealis Linux 5.2 Technical Discussion (doc_0097) X-Mailing-List: <borealis-dev@lists.penguinos.org> archive/majordomo 1.94.4 > A 1996 Award 4.51PG BIOS rolled straight back to 1900-01-01... Good catch! Note that Linux kernel `time_t` itself is a 32-bit signed integer since 1970 and won't overflow until Jan 19, 2038, so adding `hwclock --hctosys` after an `ntpdate` sync (or updating the Award BIOS EPROM) protects Borealis servers cleanly. /* POSIX time_t max = 2147483647 -> Tue Jan 19 03:14:07 2038 UTC */ -- Petr Novak | Borealis Maintainer Links...

Watch out in userland Perl 5 CGI scripts though! Half the hit counters and guestbooks on campus write `"19$year"` after `($sec,$min,$hr,$mday,$mon,$year) = localtime()`, which prints `19100` on January 1, 2000! pages.body_text: [borealis-dev] Re: ext2fs fsck - always run e2fsck -y on unmounted partition From: abrady@dialup.net (Aidan Brady) To: borealis-dev@lists.penguinos.org Date: Thu, 03 Sep 1998 22:10:10 -0700 Subject: [borealis-dev] Re: ext2fs fsck - always run e2fsck -y on unmounted partition Message-ID: <199809032210.B0110@lists.penguinos.org> X-List: Borealis Linux 5.2 Technical Discussion (doc_0110) X-Mailing-List: <borealis-dev@lists.penguinos.org> archive/majordomo 1.94.4 > Booting dropped to single-user shell with UNEXPECTED INCONSISTENCY... pages.body_text: Writing a Flat-File Perl 5 CGI Guestbook with flock() PerlMonk 5.004 Archive | Randall Mercer & Contributors | 09-Sep-1998 Flat-file CGI guestbooks routinely lose entries or zero out their data file when two Netscape visitors click Submit simultaneously. Always acquire an exclusive advisory lock with flock(FH, 2) and escape HTML angle brackets before appending. #!/usr/bin/perl -wT use strict; use CGI qw(:standard); use Fcntl qw(:flock); my $name = escapeHTML(param('name') || 'Anon'); open(my $fh, '>>', '/home/httpd/data/guestbook.txt') or die $!; flock($fh, LOCK_EX) or die $!; print $fh "$name\t" . scalar(localtime) . "\n"; close($fh); Production Note: Never skip flock() on shared campus NFS or Apache prefork servers. Independent Technical Clearinghouse Updated: 13-Sep-1998 [*] Back to The Y2K Watchtower | Section: y2k | Author: Arthur Pendelton How to Test Your PC BIOS & Real-Time Clock (1999 -> 2000 Rollover) Many 1994-1997 Pentium and 486 motherboards store only two year digits in battery-backed CMOS RTC RAM and fail to increment the century byte (0x32) across midnight Dec 31, 1999. NEVER test inside Windows 95/98 -- expired trialware and file timestamps could break! Yes (Divisible by 400) -- And Why C Code Gets It Wrong Gregorian calendar quiz: 1900 was NOT a leap year, 1800 was NOT a leap year, but 2000 IS a leap year because it is divisible by 400! Hundreds of hasty payroll and billing utilities coded the incomplete rule (year % 4 == 0 && year % 100 != 0), dropping Tuesday, February 29, 2000 entirely: /* CORRECT C90 LEAP YEAR CHECK: */ int is_leap(int year) { return (year % 4 == 0) && ((year % 100 != 0) || (year % 400 == 0)); } Also beware struct tm.tm_year (years since 1900): printing "19%02d", tm.tm_year outputs 19100! Many developers forget IBM designed EIBDATE in format 0CYYDDD+, where C is the century indicator byte (0 for 1900s, 1 for 2000s!): Dec 31, 1999 0099365+ (C=0, YY=99, DDD=365) Jan 01, 2000 0100001+ (C=1, YY=00, DDD=001) Programs using EXEC CICS FORMATTIME ABSTIME(...) YYYYMMDD(...) avoid manual century unpacking! Also keep markup clean with HTML 3.2 Wizard.
